domain: Transportation Systems / Institutional Coordination / Technology Lock-In
topic_summary: Analysis of the convention determining which side of the road vehicles travel on, focusing on right-hand driving as the dominant global standard. Examines the coordination mechanisms, path dependencies, and structural constraints that stabilize this convention despite its arbitrary origins.

key_entities.name: Left-hand traffic countries
key_entities.role: jurisdictions enforcing left-side driving convention (UK, Japan, Australia, etc.)

key_entities.name: Automotive manufacturers
key_entities.role: producers of vehicles with steering wheel placement determined by market convention

key_entities.name: Cross-border travelers
key_entities.role: drivers navigating convention transitions at jurisdictional boundaries

key_entities.name: Road infrastructure
key_entities.role: physical capital (signage, lane markings, intersections) designed for specific handedness

claims.content: The choice between right and left is structurally arbitrary—no inherent safety or efficiency advantage exists for either side in isolation
Universal adoption within a jurisdiction creates coordination value that exceeds any individual preference
Transitioning from one convention to the other requires synchronized infrastructure replacement and behavioral retraining at massive scale
The value of conforming to the dominant convention increases with the number of adopters, creating winner-take-all dynamics

tensions.nature: Jurisdictional boundaries create coordination failures where conventions collide, requiring costly adaptation infrastructure
Minority convention markets face higher vehicle costs due to economies of scale favoring majority convention

mechanisms.description: Legal penalties for driving on the wrong side enforce convention compliance
Physical road design (lane markings, signage, intersection geometry) materially constrains which side is navigable
Driver training and habituation create cognitive lock-in to local convention

absences.description: Pedestrian traffic conventions (sidewalk passing norms) are not addressed, though they may correlate with or diverge from vehicular handedness
The historical origins of the right/left split (Napoleon's military standardization, British colonial legacy) are not examined, though they explain current distribution

axes.structural_delta: The convention is self-enforcing once adopted—universal compliance creates mutual benefit that makes deviation costly for any individual actor
axes.primary_observable: Compliance rate within jurisdiction; accident rate at convention boundaries
axes.selection_reason: Upstream coordination mechanism; structurally distinct from physical and economic lock-in axes

axes.structural_delta: Road infrastructure (signage, lane geometry, intersection design) is physically built for one convention and cannot accommodate the other without reconstruction
axes.primary_observable: Capital cost of infrastructure replacement; physical compatibility of road design with opposite-side driving
axes.selection_reason: Physical constraint distinct from coordination mechanism; upstream to switching cost synthesis

axes.structural_delta: The cost of synchronized transition (infrastructure replacement, vehicle fleet turnover, retraining, accident risk during transition) exceeds any benefit from alignment with neighboring jurisdictions
axes.primary_observable: Estimated transition cost vs GDP; historical transition examples (Sweden 1967 cost data)
axes.selection_reason: Downstream synthesis node; captures entanglement of coordination and physical constraints creating path dependency

axes.structural_delta: Minority convention jurisdictions face higher costs (vehicle manufacturing, tourism friction, trade barriers) due to economies of scale favoring the majority convention
axes.primary_observable: Vehicle price differential between RHT and LHT markets; manufacturing volume by convention
axes.selection_reason: Distinct economic extraction mechanism; independent observable from switching cost barrier

omegas.description: Do pedestrian passing conventions correlate with vehicular handedness? If divergent, does this create cognitive interference or represent independent coordination equilibria?

Are current distributions purely path-dependent (Napoleon, British Empire) or do geographic/cultural factors predict convention adoption? If contingent, the Rope of coordination may be weaker than modeled.
Could autonomous vehicles eliminate the coordination constraint by handling convention-switching automatically at borders? If so, infrastructure_lock_in may be a Piton rather than Mountain.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 1 (Operational Medium) — analysis assumes human drivers

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Four axes survived independence testing with distinct observables and epsilon sources. Coordination mechanism (rope), physical constraint (mountain), path dependency synthesis (tangled_rope), and economic extraction (snare) form coherent constraint topology.
